cat > inside_range_vs_outside_near.py <<EOF
# name: inside_range_vs_outside_near
# description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max] range (multi-example sets) minus yes-rate for targets outside the range but within 5 of the nearest example; observed > null means people fill in the range more (and penalize stepping outside it more) than the summed-similarity model predicts.
$H
def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, y = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, 1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, 1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    inside = (n >= 2) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & (d > 0)
    out = (n >= 2) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & (d <= 5)
    a = y[inside].mean() if inside.any() else 0.0
    b = y[out].mean() if out.any() else 0.0
    return float(a - b)
EOF
cat > gcd_multiple_far_nodigit_rate.py <<EOF
# name: gcd_multiple_far_nodigit_rate
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples whose GCD is >=3, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of the GCD, lie >10 from every example and share no final digit with any example, minus yes-rate for comparable non-multiples; observed > null means people generalize by arithmetic rule (multiples) beyond what magnitude/digit similarity predicts.
$H
def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, y = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0).astype(int)
    g = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=int)
    for j in range(exi.shape[1]):
        g = np.gcd(g, exi[:, j])
    ti = t.astype(int)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    dig = np.any((np.mod(exi, 10) == np.mod(ti, 10)[:, None]) & ~np.isnan(ex), 1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (g >= 3) & (d > 10) & ~dig
    mult = base & (np.mod(ti, np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0)
    non = base & (np.mod(ti, np.maximum(g, 1)) != 0)
    a = y[mult].mean() if mult.any() else 0.0
    b = y[non].mean() if non.any() else 0.0
    return float(a - b)
EOF
cat > parity_contrast_far_nodigit.py <<EOF
# name: parity_contrast_far_nodigit
# description: For sets whose examples all share parity (>=2 examples), yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets, restricted to targets >10 from every example and sharing no final digit; observed > null means people use parity (even/odd) as a generalization dimension the model lacks.
$H
def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, y = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    par = np.mod(exi, 2)
    alle = np.all((par == 0) | ~valid, 1); allo = np.all((par == 1) | ~valid, 1)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    dig = np.any((np.mod(exi, 10) == np.mod(ti, 10)[:, None]) & valid, 1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (alle | allo) & (d > 10) & ~dig
    setpar = np.where(alle, 0, 1)
    same = base & (np.mod(ti, 2) == setpar)
    opp = base & (np.mod(ti, 2) != setpar)
    a = y[same].mean() if same.any() else 0.0
    b = y[opp].mean() if opp.any() else 0.0
    return float(a - b)
EOF
cat > item_yes_rate_sd.py <<EOF
# name: item_yes_rate_sd
# description: SD across (set,target) items (with >=3 responses) of the item yes-rate; observed > null means responses are more polarized/item-consistent than the model predicts (model too graded/noisy), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].agg(["mean", "count"])
    g = g[g["count"] >= 3]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())
EOF
cat > spread_endorsement_slope.py <<EOF
# name: spread_endorsement_slope
# description: Correlation across multi-example sets between the set's range (max-min) and its overall yes-rate; observed > null means wide-spread sets boost generalization more than the model's variability-tuned attention predicts, observed < null means less.
$H
def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, y = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    rng = np.nanmax(ex, 1) - np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    m = n >= 2
    s = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].to_numpy()[m], "r": rng[m], "y": y[m]})
    g = s.groupby("s").agg(r=("r", "first"), y=("y", "mean"))
    if len(g) < 3 or g["r"].std() == 0 or g["y"].std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(g["r"], g["y"])[0, 1])
EOF
cat > set_size_far_slope.py <<EOF
# name: set_size_far_slope
# description: Yes-rate on far targets (>15 from every example, no shared final digit) for 1-example sets minus that for 3-4-example sets; observed > null means people narrow generalization with more examples (size principle) more strongly than summed similarity predicts.
$H
def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, y = _parse(df)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    dig = np.any((np.mod(exi, 10) == np.mod(t.astype(int), 10)[:, None]) & valid, 1)
    far = (d > 15) & ~dig
    a = far & (n == 1); b = far & (n >= 3)
    ya = y[a].mean() if a.any() else 0.0
    yb = y[b].mean() if b.any() else 0.0
    return float(ya - yb)
EOF
cat > trial_drift.py <<EOF
# name: trial_drift
# description: Correlation between trial_index and response (yes=1) across all trials; observed differing from null means endorsement drifts over the session (e.g. growing liberal/conservative) which the stationary model does not capture.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy(); y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if x.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
EOF

I wrote all 8 test statistics to `iter_2/critique/test_stats/`. I ran each one once on the observed responses: every one returned a finite number in under 0.02 s, and none failed. Last round's statistics were thrown out for `import pandas`. These files import nothing and only use the `np`, `pd` and `math` the harness already provides. I haven't run the posterior-predictive check itself; the pipeline does that.

| Statistic | Possible failure it targets | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `inside_range_vs_outside_near` | People say yes to targets inside the examples' range more than to targets just outside it | 0.085 |
| `gcd_multiple_far_nodigit_rate` | People generalise by a shared factor (e.g. multiples of 4), even for far targets with no shared final digit | 0.092 |
| `parity_contrast_far_nodigit` | People use even/odd as a rule, which the model has no dimension for | 0.176 |
| `item_yes_rate_sd` | Answers to the same set and target are more consistent across people than the model predicts | 0.243 |
| `spread_endorsement_slope` | Across sets, how strongly a wider spread of examples raises the overall yes-rate | 0.454 |
| `set_size_far_slope` | More examples narrow generalisation to far targets (fewer yeses) | 0.098 |
| `near_gradient_steepness` | How quickly the yes-rate falls with distance from the nearest example | 0.029 |
| `trial_drift` | People get more or less willing to say yes as the session goes on; the model assumes no change | 0.026 |

For every statistic, an observed value above the model's average means people show more of that pattern than the model predicts. Each file's `# description:` line says so, so the next round can read the direction directly.
